876.title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
876.hook: Arjuna falls, then Bhima, who asks with his last breath why he is falling
876.carry: you ate without a thought for others
876.tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
876.howItsDone: The falls of Arjuna and Bhima are told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva; in recitations and retellings, the image of Yudhishthira walking on alone with the dog leads into the episode at Indra's chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday the twins fell: Sahadeva for thinking no one his equal in wisdom, Nakula in beauty. Your line was no one is equal to me.

Arjuna, who threw his bow into the sea, is still walking. He's the one who heard the Gita in the chariot, who won Draupadi at her bridegroom-choice, who fought through the war. Then, on the high road, grief at his brothers' falling seems to catch up with him, and Arjuna falls too. Bhima, who has asked why each time, asks again. A little later Bhima the strong feels his own legs go, and lying on the ground, he calls out one more question, this time about himself.
screen: `ARJUNA STILL WALKING.` → `ARJUNA FALLS.` → `BHIMA ASKS ABOUT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: About Arjuna, Yudhishthira's answer in Ganguli's telling has two parts. Arjuna once said he would destroy all their enemies in a single day, and he didn't. And he looked down on other bowmen. A boast that went unkept, and a habit of disregard. Then Bhima falls, and this time he asks about no one else: I'm falling too. Why? Yudhishthira answers him directly. You ate too much, he says, you boasted of your strength, and you ate without a thought for what others needed. Then he walks on. Now look back down this whole road. Draupadi, the twins, Arjuna, Bhima. Each fall comes with a reason, and each reason is small and specific: a heart that leaned, a comparison, a boast, an appetite. Not one of them is a great crime. These are people who did great things and, in this telling, carried one ordinary weight too many up a mountain. One more detail. Bhima, the brother who kept stopping to look, is the last to fall before Yudhishthira is alone. The question why goes with him. The text leaves no verdict on the verdicts, only an image: one man, still walking, toward the top of the world. And behind him, the only one left, not a brother, not a queen: the dog.
screen: `ARJUNA: AN UNKEPT BOAST` · `BHIMA: "WHY AM I FALLING?"` · `EACH REASON SMALL AND SPECIFIC` · then, large: `ONE MAN WALKING, AND A DOG`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle low and gently ask Bhima's question of yourself: what's one ordinary weight I'm carrying that I don't need, an old boast, a grudge, a habit of too much? Let just one come, name it on the in-breath, set it down on the path on the out-breath, and sit with the lighter feeling without hurrying on. If you pray, you can offer that weight in your prayer.
Bhima. The second Pandava, the strong one, who asks why each traveler falls, and falls last himself before Yudhishthira walks on with only the dog.
Your line: you ate without a thought for others. Now only Yudhishthira and the dog walk on. Day eight hundred seventy-six, done.

877.title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
877.hook: at the top of the world, a god offers Yudhishthira heaven, on one condition: leave the dog behind
877.carry: he will not give it up
877.tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
877.howItsDone: The story of Yudhishthira and the dog comes from the Mahaprasthanika Parva of the Mahabharata; Hindus hear it in recitations and retellings of the epic, and some retellers draw from it a lesson in loyalty and dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna fell, then Bhima, each for one small, specific weight, and Yudhishthira walked on with only the dog. Your line was you ate without a thought for others.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE THEY FALL.`

segments.voice: Two of them are left on the mountain: a king and a dog. Yudhishthira's brothers have fallen behind him. Draupadi has fallen. The dog that joined them at the start of the road is still at his heel. Then the sky fills with sound, and Indra, king of the gods, pulls up in a chariot. Climb in, he says. Heaven is waiting. This is the moment the whole road has led to. And in Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira's first answer is not yes. It's a question about who gets to come with him.
screen: `A KING AND A DOG.` → `INDRA'S CHARIOT ARRIVES.` → `"CLIMB IN."`

segments.voice: First he asks about his brothers and Draupadi; he won't go without them. Indra reassures him: they left their bodies on the way and are already in heaven. You, he says, will go up in yours. Then Yudhishthira says the dog has been devoted to him, and it should come too. Indra says no. You have won heaven and a state like a god's. Leave the dog; there is no cruelty in that. Heaven has no place for people with dogs. Notice how reasonable it sounds. It's only a dog, the offer is enormous, and no one but him will speak for it. Yudhishthira refuses. Turning away one who is devoted to you, who is frightened and has nowhere else to go, he says, is a grave wrong, and he will not give it up even for his own happiness. Then the dog changes. It is Dharma, the god of righteousness, Yudhishthira's own father, walking beside him in disguise. Dharma praises him, and recalls an earlier test at a forest lake, when Yudhishthira was asked to choose one brother to bring back to life and chose Nakula, the son of his other mother, out of fairness. Now he has chosen again, for a dog. Only then does he climb into the chariot. A long epic, full of wars, and this examination is very small: whether a king will keep faith with a creature that can't repay him.
screen: `"NOT WITHOUT MY BROTHERS"` · `INDRA: LEAVE THE DOG` · `"I WILL NOT TURN IT AWAY"` · then, large: `THE DOG IS DHARMA`

878.title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
878.hook: Yudhishthira reaches heaven and finds his old enemy enthroned there, and his brothers nowhere in sight
878.howItsDone: The Svargarohana Parva is the last book of the Mahabharata; Hindus hear its ending in recitations of the full epic, and some retellings of the epic linger on Yudhishthira's choice to stay with his family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dog at heaven's gate turned out to be Dharma, and Yudhishthira had refused to leave it. Your line was he will not give it up.

The chariot sets him down in heaven, and the first face Yudhishthira sees is Duryodhana's. The cousin behind the rigged game of dice. The man who had Draupadi dragged into the hall. The one who would not make peace. He sits in splendor, honored among the gods. Yudhishthira's brothers are nowhere. Draupadi is nowhere. Karna is nowhere. And the man who refused heaven's chariot rather than abandon a dog says, in effect, that he does not want this heaven. Take me to my brothers. Wherever they are, that's where I want to be.
screen: `DURYODHANA, ENTHRONED.` → `NO BROTHERS. NO DRAUPADI.` → `"TAKE ME TO THEM."`

segments.voice: The sage Narada tries to calm him: this is heaven, old quarrels end here, and Duryodhana died fighting as a warrior. Yudhishthira won't be calmed. So the gods send a messenger to guide him to his family. The path turns dark and smells of decay. Thorns, burning things, bodies, a river that scalds. It is a hell. Yudhishthira turns to go back, and voices call out of the dark. Stay, they beg. While you stand here, a cool breeze blows and our pain eases. Who are you? Karna, they answer. Bhima. Arjuna. Nakula. Sahadeva. Dhrishtadyumna. Draupadi. The sons of Draupadi. Everyone he loved is in torment, while the man who caused the war sits on a throne. Yudhishthira is furious, at the gods and at dharma itself. Then he chooses. He sends the messenger back without him: if his presence comforts them, he will stay in hell. That is the moment it ends. Indra and the gods appear, and the darkness lifts. It was an illusion, Indra explains; every king must glimpse hell, and Yudhishthira saw it because of his own deception in the war, about Drona's son. Dharma says his son has been tested once more and has held. Yudhishthira bathes in the heavenly Ganga, leaves his human body, and finds his brothers and Draupadi in their own true forms. The serial that began with a family quarrel ends with a man who would rather share his family's pain than enjoy a heaven without them.
screen: `NARADA: OLD QUARRELS END HERE` · `VOICES IN THE DARK: "STAY"` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY IN HELL` · then, large: `THE ILLUSION LIFTS`

879.title: the birth
879.hook: a wedding procession, a brother driving the bride's chariot, and a voice from the sky that turns him into a killer
879.carry: a promise made at sword point
879.howItsDone: The story of Krishna's birth is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana; Hindus hear it in recitations and festival retellings, especially around Krishna Janmashtami.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Mahabharata serial ended: Yudhishthira chose to stand in the dark beside his family. Your line was he will stay in hell. Today a new book opens, the Bhagavata Purana, and a new story: Krishna as a child.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY ENDS.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: The wedding is over and the music is still playing. Devaki, a princess of the Yadu clan, has just married Vasudeva. Her cousin Kamsa, a prince of Mathura, wants to honor her, so he takes the reins and drives the bridal chariot himself. Conches, drums, gifts of horses and elephants. A happy brother on a happy day. Then, the Bhagavata says, a voice speaks out of the sky, without a body, straight at the driver. Fool. The eighth child of the woman you are driving will kill you.
screen: `A WEDDING CHARIOT.` → `KAMSA HOLDS THE REINS.` → `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Kamsa grabs his cousin by the hair and draws his sword. The procession stops dead. And here is the first surprise: Vasudeva doesn't fight. He talks, gently. Death comes to everyone who is born, he says, today or in a hundred years. Killing a woman, your own sister, on her wedding day won't change that. It will only stain you. Kamsa won't listen. So Vasudeva thinks fast and makes a terrible bargain to save his wife's life right now. I'll bring you every son she bears. They're the danger, not her. Kamsa knows Vasudeva keeps his word, and he lowers the sword. And Vasudeva does keep it. When their first son is born, he carries the baby to Kamsa himself, and the text praises him: a man who holds to truth even when it costs everything. For a moment Kamsa is moved. Only the eighth child is my danger, he says; take this one home. The mercy doesn't last. The sage Narada visits Kamsa and stirs up his fear, and Kamsa locks Devaki and Vasudeva in a prison and begins to kill their children. So Krishna's story begins not with a cradle but with a promise made at sword point, and a father who keeps it. The book that will be full of a child's laughter starts in a prison cell.
screen: `THE SWORD COMES OUT` · `VASUDEVA REASONS WITH KAMSA` · `"I'LL BRING YOU EVERY SON"` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT, A PRISON CELL`

880.title: the birth
880.hook: in Kamsa's prison, a child is quietly moved from one mother to another, and the gods come to sing to an unborn baby
880.howItsDone: The prayer the gods offer to the child in Devaki's womb, told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book, is heard when the Bhagavata is recited, and Balarama is honored alongside Krishna in temples and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday the birth began at a wedding: a voice from the sky, Kamsa's sword, and Vasudeva's promise, kept. Your line was a promise made at sword point.

In the prison, Kamsa kills Devaki's children as they are born. The Bhagavata doesn't linger there. When six have died, the text says, a seventh child begins to grow in her. And this time something is done in secret. The Lord, the Bhagavata says, calls on his own power of illusion, Yogamaya, and gives her a task. A child is in danger. Move him.
screen: `A PRISON IN MATHURA.` → `THE SEVENTH CHILD.` → `"MOVE HIM."`

segments.voice: Yogamaya draws the seventh child out of Devaki's womb and places him in the womb of Rohini, another wife of Vasudeva, living safely in Gokula, a village of cowherds across the river. In the prison, people say Devaki has miscarried. In Gokula, the child grows in secret. The Bhagavata names him from that night: Sankarshana, the one who was drawn out. Later he is known as Balarama, Krishna's older brother. So the first rescue in this story is quiet and invisible. Then the Lord himself, the text says, first enters Vasudeva's mind, and from there passes into Devaki, and she begins to shine. Kamsa sees her glowing and understands: this is the one. But he can't bring himself to kill a pregnant woman, his own cousin, so he waits, and the waiting turns into obsession. Sitting, lying down, eating, walking, the text says, Kamsa saw that child everywhere. His fear made him think of the Lord constantly. And while Kamsa paces, the gods come. Brahma, Shiva and the others stand in the cell to sing praise to the child inside Devaki. Do not be afraid, mother, they tell her. The one in your womb has come to protect the world. A dark cell, a frightened mother, a jailer outside, and the whole sky gathered around someone who hasn't been born yet.

881.title: the birth
881.hook: at midnight in a dark prison, a child appears with four arms, and his mother asks him to look like an ordinary baby
881.carry: he becomes small enough to hold
881.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Krishna's birth at Janmashtami, and in homes and temples some devotees keep watch until midnight, the hour the Bhagavata gives for the birth, and then celebrate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before the birth: Balarama moved in secret to Rohini, Devaki shining in the prison, the gods singing to a child not yet born. Your line was the gods come to sing.

The Bhagavata sets the scene slowly, as if it doesn't want to rush the night. The sky is clear. The rivers run clean. Lotuses open on the lakes, birds and bees fill the woods with sound, and a cool, fragrant breeze moves. The sacred fires of the brahmanas burn bright and steady. And in the middle of the night, in deep darkness, inside a locked cell in Mathura, the text says, the Lord appears from Devaki the way the full moon rises in the east.
screen: `A CLEAR SKY, CLEAN RIVERS.` → `MIDNIGHT, DEEP DARKNESS.` → `LIKE THE FULL MOON RISING.`

segments.voice: Vasudeva looks at the newborn, and it is not an ordinary baby. The child has four arms, holding a conch, a mace, a discus and a lotus. A jewel shines at his throat. He wears yellow silk. Vasudeva knows exactly who this is. He folds his hands and praises him: you are beyond all things, and you have come into this house. Then Devaki speaks. Her praise is lovely, and then it turns very practical, very much a mother's. Please, hide this form. Kamsa must not know you were born here. And this shape, with the conch and discus, is too much for ordinary eyes. Become small. The Lord answers with a secret. He has been their child before. In an earlier age they spent long years in austerity asking for a son like him, and he was born to them. Then again in another life. Now this is the third time. Remember me as your son, he tells them, and you will reach me. Then, while they watch, he does what his mother asked. The four arms, the jewel, the radiance: gone. On the prison floor lies a newborn, like any other. That is the heart of the birth in this telling. The Lord of the universe arrives at full height, and the first thing he does, at his mother's request, is make himself small enough to be held and hidden. In this telling, the childhood stories to come, the butter, the mischief, the cowherds, grow out of that one choice.

882.title: the crossing of the Yamuna
882.hook: the guards fall asleep, the bolted doors swing open, and Vasudeva walks out into a storm carrying a newborn
882.howItsDone: The crossing of the Yamuna is retold at Janmashtami in songs, plays and temple tableaux, and the image of Vasudeva carrying the infant through the river under Shesha's hoods is a familiar one in Hindu art.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth: four arms at midnight, and then, at Devaki's request, an ordinary baby on the prison floor. Your line was he becomes small enough to hold.

The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. Prompted by the Lord himself, the Bhagavata says, Vasudeva picks up his son, and the prison starts to come undone. The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low. Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river.

segments.voice: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, through a storm, at night. The Bhagavata adds two details. First, the rain. Shesha, the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, follows behind Vasudeva and spreads his hoods over father and child like an umbrella. The cosmic serpent, holding off the weather for a newborn. Then the river. The Yamuna that night is swollen and fast, full of waves, whirlpools and foam, deep enough to stop anyone. And the river makes way, the text says, as the ocean once gave way for Rama when he crossed to Lanka to bring back Sita. The same Lord, another age, another stretch of water opening. Later retellings add more: in some, Vasudeva carries the baby in a basket on his head; in some, the river rises to touch the child's feet before it parts. The Bhagavata's own account is shorter: the father, the child, the serpent, the river giving way. Look back over this week and the same shape keeps returning. Yudhishthira refusing to leave a dog. Yudhishthira staying in the dark with his family. Vasudeva keeping a terrible promise. Now Vasudeva, walking into a flood with a baby. Help arrives in this week's stories, but someone still has to walk.
